fields.tagline: Rock mechanics · Slope stability & landslides · Numerical modelling
fields.bio:
I am a Senior Scientist and Leader of the Rock Mechanics Group at the Chair of Engineering Geology and Hydrogeology, RWTH Aachen University. My research focuses on rock mechanics, rock engineering design and numerical modelling, applied to rock slope and landslide analysis and to underground infrastructure, from the laboratory to the in-situ scale.

I have been principal investigator and co-investigator on national and international projects on deep geological repositories, rock slope stability and landslide analysis, geohazard assessment and underground excavation design.

I teach Soil & Rock Mechanics, Landslides and Rock Slope Analysis, Underground Excavation, Dams and Hydroelectric Power Plants, and field excursions. I am a member of the International Society for Rock Mechanics (ISRM) and the American Rock Mechanics Association (ARMA), and a reviewer for Rock Mechanics and Rock Engineering, Landslides, and the Journal of Rock Mechanics and Geotechnical Engineering.

fields.title: Progressive Excavation Disturbance Zone Evolution during and Post Mine-by Tunnelling (PRECODE)
fields.summary: A 100 m experimental tunnel branching off the Bedretto tunnel in Ticino, Switzerland, instrumented to monitor strain, pore pressure and micro-seismicity. The project studies how the excavation damage zone forms and evolves, long-term fracture propagation, permeability changes and the impact on fault zones. Partners: York University, Dalhousie University, ETH Zurich and BGE Tech.
fields.partners: York University (Canada), Dalhousie University (Canada), ETH Zurich (Switzerland), BGE Tech (Germany)
fields.body:
Fracture initiation and propagation in the surrounding of tunnel excavations in highly stressed rocks may initiate during the tunnelling process and develop over time. This progressive brittle fracturing may lead to an interconnected fracture network, typically associated with the radiation of micro-seismic signals. Within the excavation damage zone (EDZ), the permeability is often enhanced by two to three orders of magnitude and, in the framework of nuclear waste disposal, may provide preferential pathways for radionuclide migration.

Within the PRECODE experiment, we investigate the development and time-dependent changes around a tunnel at the Bedretto Underground Laboratory for Geosciences and Geoenergies (BULGG) in Ticino, Switzerland. The infrastructure and experimental design will be integrated with ongoing projects at LIH, such as the FEAR and SPINE experiments. Within PRECODE we will establish a new, 100 m long experimental tunnel as a branch from the existing Bedretto tunnel, which will be densely instrumented with strain, pore pressure and micro-seismic sensors prior to the excavation.

The main objectives of the PRECODE experiment are to understand:

1. Short-term rock mass behaviour and EDZ formation during tunnelling
2. Long-term fracture propagation within the EDZ associated with environmental conditions
3. Permeability changes with time around an open excavation
4. The impact of tunnelling on dislocations across nearby fault zones

fields.title: Understanding Failure Mechanism of Non-Persistent Discontinuities Using 3D-Printed Synthetic Rock Mass
fields.summary: Laboratory tests on 3D-printed synthetic rock mass samples with known joint configurations, used to calibrate numerical models and develop a constitutive model for rock mass strength. In collaboration with GeoPrint at the University of Alberta, Canada.
fields.partners: GeoPrint at the University of Alberta, Canada
fields.body:
DFG project number 463538034.

Rock mass consists of a complex interplay of two components: the intact rock and spatially distributed rock joints of various orientation and persistence. It is of paramount importance to understand rock mass behaviour in geo-engineering, as an adequate design of structures such as tunnels and slopes relies on the rock mass strength and deformation characteristics. There is currently no direct way of estimating the mechanical characteristics of rock mass, and it is common in practice to estimate rock mass strength indirectly using empirical classification.

The aim of this project is to understand the mechanical characteristics and failure mechanism of rock mass through additive manufacturing (3D printing). Using 3D printing, we build synthetic rock mass samples with known configurations (the strength and the spatial distribution of rock joints) and test them systematically in the laboratory. The key advantage of this method is that it allows repeatable laboratory testing on samples with similar physical conditions, reducing uncertainty and increasing the reliability of results.

The results of the laboratory tests on the 3D-printed samples are then used to calibrate and verify numerical results, with the goal of developing a new constitutive model to estimate rock mass strength.

fields.title: Landslide Dam Properties and Stability (LADY)
fields.summary: Why do some landslide dams remain stable for thousands of years while others fail within months? LADY combines dam mapping, lake water-balance analysis and numerical stability simulations to test a new hypothesis.
fields.role: Principal Investigator (with Anja Dufresne and Florian Amann)
fields.body:
Research on natural dams at LIH has been running since 2016.

Large landslides occur both in mountainous regions and where rivers incise the landscape (for example, the vast plains of the Peace River region in British Columbia, Canada). They can completely block a valley, dam the river, and form lakes whose stability varies from minutes to millennia.

Research at LIH includes regional studies to examine the longevity of landslide dams, test empirical stability criteria in different materials, landslide types and environments, and illuminate their long-term landscape impacts (Dufresne et al. 2018; Miller et al. 2018).

Based on two review articles (Fan et al. 2020 and 2021), a comprehensive database of landslide dams from around the world is being developed in preparation for a Springer book (Dufresne, Fan, Wolter, editors: *Landslide Dams Around the World*). In the book, the database will be expanded with additional data entries and analyses, and treated in geographic chapters. An international team of co-authors and interested parties met at EGU 2023 in a session on the topic.

In our new DFG-funded project, LADY (Landslide Dam Properties and Stability), our goal is to understand why some landslide dams maintain stable lakes for up to thousands of years while others fail within minutes to a few months of their formation. Much is still unknown about the exact failure processes, and understanding of dam performance varies widely between disciplines. This project aims to fill this gap by bringing together expertise from landslide sedimentology, dam construction, hydrology and numerical analysis. Detailed dam mapping will be combined with engineering approaches, lake water-balance assessment, numerical simulation of dam stability, and testing of a new hypothesis. With this multidisciplinary approach, we expect to deepen our knowledge of the processes involved in the failure of natural dams and advance our understanding of their stability.

Einstein Telescope EMR Site & Technology (E-TEST)
fields.summary: Feasibility study and geological inventory of the subsurface in the Euregio Meuse-Rhine to find a site for the Einstein Telescope gravitational-wave observatory. Led by the University of Liège with 11 universities and institutions from Belgium, the Netherlands and Germany.
fields.role: Principal Investigator at RWTH (with Florian Amann)
fields.partners: University of Liège (lead), UCLouvain, UHasselt, KU Leuven, RWTH Aachen University, Fraunhofer ILT, University of Bonn, NMWP, Maastricht University, KNMI, Nikhef
fields.body:
The Einstein Telescope (ET) is an advanced gravitational-wave observatory, currently in the planning stage, that will further our understanding of the Universe through the observation of gravitational waves. The border region between the Netherlands, Belgium and Germany (Euregio Meuse-Rhine) is being considered as a possible location because of its tranquillity and stable ground. The ET involves the construction of a triangular underground facility with 10 km long arms at a depth of 200–300 m below the surface. The underground structure will host multiple laser interferometers, each of which can detect ripples in the fabric of space-time. As an initial step, a feasibility study is carried out to determine whether the Einstein Telescope can be built in the Euregio Meuse-Rhine.

The E-TEST project is carried out within the framework of the [Interreg V-A Euregio Meuse-Rhine](https://www.interregemr.eu/projekte/e-test-de) programme, which is supported by the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF) with 7.5 million euros. By allocating EU funds to Interreg projects, the European Union invests directly in economic development, innovation, territorial development, social inclusion and education in the Euregio Meuse-Rhine. Further funding is provided by the Dutch Ministry of Economic Affairs, the State of North Rhine-Westphalia, the Province of Flemish Brabant, the Province of Belgian Limburg, the Province of Dutch Limburg, Flanders and Wallonia.

Under the leadership of the University of Liège, 11 universities and research institutions from Belgium, the Netherlands and Germany carry out the feasibility study. For this purpose, E-TEST takes an inventory of the underground in the Euregio Meuse-Rhine. The geological investigations started in mid-2020 and were planned to be completed by the end of 2022. A monitoring system and a geological model will be set up, allowing geological aspects such as groundwater levels and earthquakes to be modelled, simulated and predicted. The aim of the project is to find the best possible location for the Einstein Telescope in the Euregio Meuse-Rhine.

fields.title: Rock Slope Response to Glacier Retreat (Grewingk Glacier and Lake, Alaska)
fields.role: Principal Investigator (with Anja Dufresne and Florian Amann)
fields.body:
## Tsunamigenic landslides

Project term: 2016 to 2020. Contact: [Anja Dufresne](https://www.lih.rwth-aachen.de/cms/LIH/Der-Lehrstuhl/Team/Ingenieurgeologie/~qfrk/Anja-Dufresne/lidx/1/).

At least 24 large rock slope failures have occurred in Glacier Bay National Park in SE Alaska since 1984, as reported by Coe et al. (2018). The resulting rock avalanches cover areas between 5.5 and 22.2 km². Two of these events are studied by research groups that Anja Dufresne from the Department of Engineering Geology is collaborating with.

## The 2015 rock slope failure and tsunami in Icy Bay

The October 2015 Tyndall Glacier rock avalanche caused one of the largest historic tsunamis in Alaska; the maximum wave runup height measured from field evidence was 192 m (Haeussler et al. 2017; Dufresne et al. 2018; Higman et al. 2018). Located in the remote Taan Fiord, an arm of Icy Bay, no people or infrastructure were affected, nor would this event have been noticed if it hadn't been recorded by the long-period seismic event detector at Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory of Columbia University in New York (cf. Ekström and Stark 2013). The slope it originated from has shown signs of deformation since at least 1996 (Meigs et al. 2006); its catastrophic failure in 2015 released some 76 million m³ of rock, most of which now lies beneath fjord waters. A rapid response by an NSF-funded group of international researchers in the summer of 2016 gathered data, including bathymetry, aerial photographs, a high-resolution DEM, and structural and sedimentological field data, which only a few months later was already altered or destroyed by erosion, sedimentation and/or advance of the glacier terminus (Dufresne et al. 2018).

Material Approach for Opalinus Clay
fields.summary: Development and validation of a hydro-mechanical constitutive model for Opalinus Clay, based on laboratory triaxial tests and implemented in MOOSE.
fields.body:
Opalinus Clay, a Mesozoic shale formation, has been selected as the potential host rock for the disposal of high- and low-level nuclear waste in Switzerland. Beneficial characteristics of this formation include its low hydraulic conductivity, high radionuclide retention potential, and the potential for self-sealing of open cracks and fissures.

The aim of this project is to develop a fully coupled hydro-mechanical (HM) constitutive model to predict the physical behaviour of Opalinus Clay under various loading and unloading conditions. The key aspect is to integrate existing HM-coupled models supported by laboratory tests, field experiments and numerical simulations, and to develop, implement and validate a new constitutive model.

## Phase 1.0 (2018–2022)

### Experimental investigations

In the first phase of this project, we performed HM-coupled experiments using our state-of-the-art laboratory machines. We used our in-house technology to prepare, store, monitor and perform, for instance, drained or undrained triaxial compression tests under various configurations considering the material anisotropy. Post-failure analyses were carried out by analysing the deformation structures using electron microscopy.

### Numerical investigations

A transversely isotropic elasto-plastic model coupled with damage was implemented in the finite element code MOOSE Framework to describe the hydro-mechanical behaviour of Opalinus Clay. The model describes four deformation regimes observed in consolidated-undrained tests: (1) transversely isotropic elastic deformation, (2) plastic deformation with cross-anisotropic peak strength, (3) the post-failure regime, and (4) the residual strength state.

### Main results of phase 1.0

An extensive testing campaign was conducted on Opalinus Clay specimens from the shaly facies sampled at the Mont Terri URL. Hydraulic properties were determined using different experimental methods, including the pore pressure oscillation technique, and the methods were evaluated in terms of their applicability, robustness and experimental times. Rock mechanical strength tests were performed for different suction values and different loading orientations. Furthermore, triaxial tests under consolidated-undrained conditions were performed under various boundary conditions to investigate the effect of effective stress and loading angle. Electron microscopy was carried out to study the microscale deformation processes and link the bulk hydro-mechanical observations to the underlying mechanics at the sub-millimetre level. The large amount of experimental data and analyses contributed substantially to the calibration of the new constitutive model and the implementation of fundamental behaviour characteristics of Opalinus Clay.

A non-associated plastic model was implemented in the MOOSE Framework and coupled with a non-local damage model to describe the failure and post-failure behaviour of Opalinus Clay under undrained conditions. A series of consolidated-undrained experiments was used to calibrate the model and determine the required parameters for P-, Z- and S-specimens from the shaly facies of the Mont Terri URL. A large-scale 3D tunnel model was also developed to evaluate the performance of the implemented constitutive model against existing field data, such as pore pressure evolution, deformations and the excavation damage zone (EDZ).

## Phase 2.0 (2022–2025)

### Experimental investigations

In the second phase of this project, we perform long-term THM-coupled triaxial experiments to observe the time-dependent deformation behaviour of fully saturated samples under drained conditions. As in the first phase, the deformed specimens will be subjected to microstructural analysis (BIB-SEM) for a better understanding of creep mechanisms at the microscale in clay rocks. Multistage creep tests will be conducted considering the structural anisotropy and the effect of temperature on creep behaviour. Specimens with the bedding oriented either parallel or perpendicular to the loading axis will be tested under elevated temperature conditions. Additionally, sample material from the EDZ will be the subject of creep investigations to analyse the influence of damage on long-term creep behaviour.

### Numerical investigations

The existing constitutive model will be calibrated against experiments performed on sample material from greater depth, i.e. from higher effective consolidation stresses. Additionally, a creep model will be implemented in MOOSE to simulate the time-dependent deformation observed in the creep tests. The focus will mainly be on steady-state and tertiary creep deformation under the influence of stress and temperature.

A retrogressive landslide in the Peace River region, British Columbia, Canada, blocked a small river and continues to deliver high sediment loads to the river network.

The Einstein Telescope gravitational-wave observatory will be situated at a depth of 200–300 m in the Euregio Meuse-Rhine landscape. The triangular underground facility with 10 km long arms allows for the installation of multiple laser interferometers.

On 17 October 2015, a landslide of roughly 180 million tons of rock landed on the toe of Tyndall Glacier and in the water of Taan Fiord. It sent a tsunami wave that reached as high as 193 m on the opposite valley slopes.
